overview:
Pañcāstikāya (often spelled Panchastikaya or Pañcāstikāya-sāra) is a foundational metaphysical text and concept in Jain philosophy, especially within the Digambara tradition. As a concept, pañcāstikāya refers to the "five asti-kāyas"—five eternal, extended substances that possess both existence (asti) and body or extension (kāya). As a text, Pañcāstikāya-saṃgraha or Pañcāstikāya-sāra is a Prakrit work traditionally attributed to Ācārya Kundakunda (circa 1st century BCE–1st century CE), one of the most influential Digambara ācāryas. It systematically expounds Jain metaphysics: the nature of substance (dravya), qualities (guṇa), modes (paryāya), and the structure of the universe.

In Jain ontology, reality is analyzed in terms of substances (dravya) that are characterized by both permanence and change. A substance remains itself (sattā) while undergoing origination (utpāda), destruction (vyaya), and continuity (dhrauvya). Pañcāstikāya focuses on those substances that are "astikāya"—they exist and occupy multiple space-points (pradeśa), thus having a kind of "body" or extension. These five are: jīva (soul), pudgala (matter), dharma (medium of motion), adharma (medium of rest), and ākāśa (space). Together, they constitute the loka, the universe-space in which worldly existence and karmic bondage occur.

Kundakunda’s Pañcāstikāya-saṃgraha explains that outside the loka lies aloka, the non-universe-space, which consists solely of pure space (ākāśa) without the other four astikāyas. Time (kāla) is acknowledged as a sixth substance in broader Jain metaphysics, but it is explicitly excluded from the category of astikāya because it occupies only a single space-point and therefore lacks bodily extension. This distinction between astikāya substances and non-astikāya time is central to the technical meaning of pañcāstikāya.

The text and the doctrine are closely tied to other core Jain categories: the six substances (ṣaḍ-dravya: jīva, pudgala, dharma, adharma, ākāśa, kāla), the seven tattvas (fundamental realities), the nine padārthas (objects of philosophical analysis), and the doctrine of conditional predication (syādvāda) with its sevenfold schema (saptabhaṅgī). Pañcāstikāya thus serves as a bridge between abstract metaphysical analysis and the soteriological path, because understanding the nature of jīva and its relation to pudgala and the cosmic media is essential for grasping bondage (bandha), influx (āsrava), stoppage (saṃvara), and liberation (mokṣa).

Each of the five astikāyas has a distinct role:

- Jīva is the conscious, sentient substance, capable of knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy in its pure state. It is infinite in number and present in all living beings—from one-sensed organisms to omniscient liberated souls (siddhas). In its worldly condition (saṃsārī jīva), it is bound by karmic pudgala.
- Pudgala is matter, ranging from gross bodies and physical objects to subtle karmic particles. It alone has form, color, taste, smell, and touch, and it is the only substance that directly interacts with jīva to form karmic bondage.
- Dharma-dravya is the medium of motion, not moral righteousness but a cosmic principle that enables movement of jīva and pudgala within the universe, analogous to water enabling fish to swim.
- Adharma-dravya is the medium of rest, enabling beings and matter to remain still, analogous to shade allowing a traveler to stop and rest.
- Ākāśa is space, providing accommodation for all other substances and differentiating loka (universe-space) from aloka (non-universe-space).

Pañcāstikāya emphasizes that these substances are eternal, mutually interrelated, and characterized by inseparable association of substance and qualities. It also underscores the distinction between conscious (jīva) and non-conscious (ajīva) substances, a key duality in Jain metaphysics. By clarifying what truly exists and how it exists, the pañcāstikāya framework supports the Jain ethical and spiritual project: recognizing the soul’s difference from matter, understanding the conditions of bondage, and orienting practice toward the realization of the pure, liberated jīva.

Modern expositions of Pañcāstikāya, drawing on traditional commentaries and contemporary scholarship, highlight its role as a concise yet profound summary of Jain metaphysics. It is often studied alongside Kundakunda’s other major works—Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, and Niyamasāra—and with the Tattvārtha-sūtra of Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi, which is authoritative for both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. Together, these texts provide a multi-layered understanding of reality that integrates logical analysis, doctrinal precision, and spiritual aspiration.

primary_sources.title: Pañcāstikāya-saṃgraha (Pañcāstikāya-sāra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
जिवपुग्गलधम्माधम्माकासाया पंचअस्तिकाया लोहो।
एत्थ लोहो तव्वो, तव्वो लोहो, तव्वस्स लोहो तव्वं॥ (indicative of verses describing the five astikāyas and loka)

Note: Exact Prakrit wording varies by edition; here only representative lines are indicated.
primary_sources.transliteration:
jivapuggala-dhammā-dhammākāsāyā pañca-astikāyā loho.
ettha loho tavvo, tavvo loho, tavvassa loho tavvaṃ.

(Representative transliteration; consult a critical edition for precise text.)
primary_sources.translation:
“The universe (loka) consists of five astikāyas: soul (jīva), matter (pudgala), the medium of motion (dharma), the medium of rest (adharma), and space (ākāśa). Here, the universe is a substance, and the substance is the universe; the universe is the mode of the substance, and the substance is the mode of the universe.”

This captures the doctrinal point that loka is constituted by the five extended substances and that substance and its modes are inseparably related.
primary_sources.notes: Pañcāstikāya-saṃgraha is a Prakrit text of 173 verses attributed to Ācārya Kundakunda. It is one of his four principal works, along with Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, and Niyamasāra. The text systematically presents the five astikāyas, their characteristics, and their role in constituting the universe-space (loka). It explicitly distinguishes kāla (time) as a dravya that is not an astikāya because it occupies only a single space-point and lacks bodily extension. Modern editions, such as those with English explanatory notes by Vijay K. Jain, provide critical text, transliteration, and commentary based on traditional Digambara exegesis.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (particularly Chapter 5: The Non-living Substances)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.original_text:
द्रव्याणि ॥ ५.२ ॥
धर्माधर्माकाशपुद्गला द्रव्याणि ॥

अजीवकाया ॥ ५.१ ॥
धर्माधर्माकाशपुद्गलकालाः अजीवकाया ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
dravyāṇi || 5.2 ||
dharmādharmākāśapudgalā dravyāṇi ||

ajīvakāyā || 5.1 ||
dharmādharmākāśapudgalākālāḥ ajīvakāyā ||
primary_sources.translation:
“Substances (dravya) (5.2): Dharma, adharma, space (ākāśa), and matter (pudgala) are substances.”

“Non-soul aggregates (ajīva-kāya) (5.1): Dharma, adharma, space, matter, and time are non-soul aggregates.”

These sūtras, together with others in Chapter 5, classify the non-living substances and clarify their functions as media of motion and rest, space, matter, and time.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha-sūtra is a Sanskrit aphoristic text accepted as authoritative by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. While it does not use the term pañcāstikāya explicitly in the same way as Kundakunda’s text, it provides the broader framework of six substances (ṣaḍ-dravya) and distinguishes jīva from ajīva. Commentaries such as Sarvārthasiddhi by Ācārya Pūjyapāda elaborate on the definition of dravya, the inseparability of substance and qualities, and the specific roles of dharma, adharma, ākāśa, pudgala, and kāla. These discussions underpin the pañcāstikāya doctrine by clarifying which substances are extended (astikāya) and how they function in the universe.

primary_sources.title: Dravya-saṃgraha
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta Cakravartin (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
जिवाजिवा दुविहा दव्वा।
जिवो उवओगो अमूर्तो कर्ता सव्वकम्माणं।
भोक्क्ता सव्वफलाणं संसारस्स सिद्धो उव्वग्गो॥

पुग्गलधम्माधम्माकासकालाः अजीवा दव्वा॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
jivājivā duvihā davvā.
jivo uvayogo amūrto kartā savvakammāṇaṃ.
bhokkttā savvaphalāṇaṃ saṃsārassa siddho uvvaggo.

puggaladhammādhammākāsakālāḥ ajīvā davvā.
primary_sources.translation:
“Substances (dravya) are of two kinds: soul (jīva) and non-soul (ajīva). The soul is characterized by upayoga (conscious activity), is non-material, the doer of all actions, the enjoyer of all their fruits, existing in saṃsāra and in its perfected state (siddha), and having an upward tendency.

Matter (pudgala), dharma, adharma, space (ākāśa), and time (kāla) are non-soul substances (ajīva).”
primary_sources.notes: Dravya-saṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit/Prakrit treatise on the six substances, often studied alongside Pañcāstikāya. It clearly distinguishes jīva from the five ajīva substances and emphasizes the defining characteristics of soul as conscious and non-material. By listing pudgala, dharma, adharma, ākāśa, and kāla as ajīva dravyas, it provides the ontological basis for later Digambara elaborations on pañcāstikāya, where the first five are treated as astikāyas and kāla is excluded from that category.

primary_sources.title: Outlines of Jainism (quoting Pañcāstikāya)
primary_sources.author: Jagmanderlal Jaini (modern secondary source quoting primary Prakrit)
primary_sources.original_text:
पंचास्तिकाय, ९।
यद् यद् भावपरिणामं गच्छति तद् द्रव्यं।
सत्तातो न पृथक्।

पंचास्तिकाय, १३।
गुणा द्रव्यं न पृथक्।
न च द्रव्यं गुणेभ्यः पृथक्।
तस्मात् गुणद्रव्ययोः अविभागः।
primary_sources.transliteration:
pañcāstikāya, 9.
yad yad bhāva-pariṇāmaṃ gacchati tad dravyaṃ.
sattāto na pṛthak.

pañcāstikāya, 13.
guṇā dravyaṃ na pṛthak.
na ca dravyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ pṛthak.
tasmāt guṇa-dravyayoḥ avibhāgaḥ.
primary_sources.translation:
“Pañcāstikāya 9: That which undergoes modifications of states (bhāva-pariṇāma) is called substance (dravya). It is never distinct from existence (sattā).

Pañcāstikāya 13: Qualities (guṇa) are not separate from substance (dravya), nor is substance separate from qualities. Therefore, there is inseparability between qualities and substance.”
primary_sources.notes: These verses, cited and translated in Jagmanderlal Jaini’s ‘Outlines of Jainism’, illustrate Kundakunda’s technical definitions of dravya and the inseparability of substance and qualities. They are central to understanding how pañcāstikāya frames the five extended substances: each is a dravya characterized by its own guṇas and paryāyas, yet none can be conceived apart from its qualities and modes. While Jaini’s work is a modern secondary source, the quoted verses derive from primary Prakrit manuscripts of Pañcāstikāya.

misconceptions.myth: Pañcāstikāya refers to five moral principles or ethical vows in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Pañcāstikāya does not denote ethical vows but five metaphysical substances that possess existence and bodily extension: jīva, pudgala, dharma, adharma, and ākāśa. It is a technical ontological category, not a list of moral rules. Ethical vows (such as ahiṃsā, satya, asteya, brahmacarya, aparigraha) belong to a different doctrinal domain.

misconceptions.myth: Time (kāla) is always included among the pañcāstikāya and is the sixth astikāya.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain metaphysics, time (kāla) is indeed a substance (dravya), but it is explicitly not classified as an astikāya because it occupies only a single space-point and lacks bodily extension. Pañcāstikāya, by definition, includes only five astikāyas—jīva, pudgala, dharma, adharma, and ākāśa. Confusing the broader list of six dravyas with the narrower category of five astikāyas leads to this misconception.

misconceptions.myth: Dharma and adharma in pañcāstikāya are about righteousness and sin, like in common religious usage.
misconceptions.reality: In the context of pañcāstikāya, dharma-dravya and adharma-dravya are not moral categories but cosmic media. Dharma is the medium that enables motion, and adharma is the medium that enables rest. They are non-conscious substances that function analogously to water allowing movement and shade allowing rest. Moral dharma (right conduct) is a separate concept and should not be conflated with these metaphysical media.

misconceptions.myth: Pañcāstikāya is a purely Digambara doctrine with no relevance to Śvetāmbara Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: While the Pañcāstikāya-saṃgraha text is especially prominent in the Digambara tradition and attributed to Kundakunda, the underlying ontology of five extended substances plus time as a sixth dravya is shared across Jain traditions. Śvetāmbara authorities also accept the six dravyas and the distinction between jīva and ajīva, as seen in Tattvārtha-sūtra. The terminology and textual emphasis may differ, but the core metaphysical structure is broadly Jain, not sect-specific.
